entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4742"/><div sID="gen6892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4742"/>7. Man may the more claim a peaceful life, since, when separated from it by death, he never returns to it. This does not deny a future life, but a return to the present condition of life. Job plainly hopes for a future state (<reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job 14:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.7.2">Job 7:2</reference>). Still, it is but vague and trembling hope, not assurance; excepting the one bright glimpse in <reference osisRef="Job.19.25">Job 19:25</reference>. The Gospel revelation was needed to change fears, hopes, and glimpses into clear and definite certainties. <div eID="gen6892" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4746"/><div sID="gen6899" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4746"/><hi type="bold">12. heavens be no more--</hi>This only implies that Job had no hope of living again in the present order of the world, not that he had no hope of life again in a new order of things. <reference osisRef="Ps.102.26">Psa 102:26</reference> proves that early under the Old Testament the dissolution of the present earth and heavens was expected (compare <reference osisRef="Gen.8.22">Ge 8:22</reference>). Enoch before Job had implied that the "saints shall live again" (Jude 14; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.13-Heb.11.16">He 11:13-16</reference>). Even if, by this phrase, Job meant "never" (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">Psa 89:29</reference>) in his gloomier state of feelings, yet the Holy Ghost has made him unconsciously (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1Pe 1:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.12">12</reference>) use language expressing the truth, that the resurrection is to be preceded by the dissolution of the heavens. In <reference osisRef="Job.14.13-Job.14.15">Job 14:13-15</reference> he plainly passes to brighter hopes of a world to come. <div eID="gen6899" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 12. heavens be no more-- This only implies that Job had no hope of living again in the present order of the world, not that he had no hope of life again in a new order of things. In Job 14:13-15 he plainly passes to brighter hopes of a world to come.

Job wishes to be kept hidden in the grave until God's wrath against him shall have passed away. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4748"/><div sID="gen6902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4748"/><hi type="bold">14. shall he live?--</hi>The answer implied is, There is a hope that he shall, though not in the present order of life, as is shown by the words following. Job had denied (<reference osisRef="Job.14.10-Job.14.12">Job 14:10-12</reference>) that man shall live again in this present world. But hoping for a "set time," when God shall remember and raise him out of the hiding-place of the grave (<reference osisRef="Job.14.13">Job 14:13</reference>), he declares himself willing to "wait all the days of his appointed time" of continuance in the grave, however long and hard that may be.<div eID="gen6902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">appointed time--</hi>literally, "warfare, hard service"; imlying the hardship of being shut out from the realms of life, light, and God for the time he shall be in the grave (<reference osisRef="Job.7.1">Job 7:1</reference>).<div eID="gen6903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">change--</hi>my release, as a soldier at his post released from duty by the relieving guard (see on <reference osisRef="Job.10.17">Job 10:17</reference>) [Umbreit and Gesenius], but elsewhere Gesenius explains it, "renovation," as of plants in spring (<reference osisRef="Job.14.7">Job 14:7</reference>), but this does not accord so well with the metaphor in "appointed time" or "warfare." <div eID="gen6904" type="x-p"/>

But hoping for a "set time," when God shall remember and raise him out of the hiding-place of the grave ( Job 14:13 ), he declares himself willing to "wait all the days of his appointed time" of continuance in the grave, however long and hard that may be. appointed time-- literally, "warfare, hard service"; imlying the hardship of being shut out from the realms of life, light, and God for the time he shall be in the grave ( Job 7:1 ). change-- my release, as a soldier at his post released from duty by the relieving guard (see on Job 10:17 ) [Umbreit and Gesenius], but elsewhere Gesenius explains it, "renovation," as of plants in spring ( Job 14:7 ), but this does not accord so well with the metaphor in "appointed time" or "warfare."

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4749"/><div sID="gen6905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4749"/>15. namely, at the resurrection (<reference osisRef="John.5.28">Joh 5:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.17.15">Psa 17:15</reference>).<div eID="gen6905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">have a desire to--</hi>literally, "become pale with anxious desire:" the same word is translated "sore longedst after" (<reference osisRef="Gen.31.30">Ge 31:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">Psa 84:2</reference>), implying the utter unlikelihood that God would leave in oblivion the "creature of His own hands so fearfully and wonderfully made." It is objected that if Job knew of a future retribution, he would make it the leading topic in solving the problem of the permitted afflictions of the righteous. But, (1) He did not intend to exceed the limits of what was clearly revealed; the doctrine was then in a vague form only; (2) The doctrine of God's moral government in this life, even independently of the future, needed vindication. <div eID="gen6906" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4752"/><div sID="gen6911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4752"/><hi type="bold">18. cometh to naught--</hi>literally, "fadeth"; a poetical image from a leaf (<reference osisRef="Isa.34.4">Is 34:4</reference>). Here Job falls back into his gloomy bodings as to the grave. Instead of "and surely," translate "yet"; marking the transition from his brighter hopes. Even the solid mountain falls and crumbles away; man therefore cannot "hope" to escape decay or to live again in the present world (<reference osisRef="Job.14.19">Job 14:19</reference>).<div eID="gen6911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of his place--</hi>so man (<reference osisRef="Ps.103.16">Psa 103:16</reference>). <div eID="gen6912" type="x-p"/>

One striking trait is selected from the sad picture of the severance of the dead from all that passes in the world (<reference osisRef="Eccl.9.5">Ec 9:5</reference>), namely, the utter separation of parents and children. <div eID="gen6918" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4756"/><div sID="gen6919" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4756"/>22. "Flesh" and "soul" describe the whole man. Scripture rests the hope of a future life, not on the inherent immortality of the soul, but on the restoration of the body with the soul. In the unseen world, Job in a gloomy frame anticipates, man shall be limited to the thought of his own misery. "Pain is by personification, from our feelings while alive, attributed to the flesh and soul, as if the man could feel in his body when dead. It is the dead in general, not the wicked, who are meant here." <chapter eID="Job.14"/>
